title: Stop being whirled around
hook: don't let outside things distract you; make time to learn something good (Meditations 2.7)

segments.voice: Yesterday: throw away the thirst for books, not the books. Your line was enough reading. What did you put down, and what did you live by instead? Day five hundred thirty-three.

Eleven browser tabs. A half-written email. A notification, then another. You check the news, then the weather, then the news again, in case it changed in the last four minutes. A day like that can leave a person worn out by evening, with nothing finished to show for it. Book two has a word for that state, and it's a physical one: whirled around. Spun, like a top, or a leaf in a gust of wind. Today: stop being whirled around.
screen: `ELEVEN TABS, NO PROGRESS.` → `A LEAF IN A GUST.` → `STOP BEING WHIRLED AROUND.`

segments.voice: First, the question. Section seven opens by asking: do the things outside you distract you? Marcus was running an empire at war. If anyone had a reason to be distracted, it was him. Second, the cure. In Long's translation: "Give thyself time to learn something new and good, and cease to be whirled around." Notice the cure isn't, empty your mind. It's, give yourself something good to learn. A mind with nothing to hold onto spins. A mind with something worth learning has a center. Third, the second mistake. Then Marcus catches himself, because there's a trap on the other side. Some people, he says, wear themselves out with activity, and yet have no aim to which they direct every movement and every thought. They're busy, but they're still spinning. Being whirled around by outside things is one mistake. Whirling yourself around with aimless busyness is the other. Both look like motion. Neither goes anywhere. Fourth, the aim. What Marcus wants is a center: one aim that every movement points toward. Here he doesn't say what his own aim was. It doesn't have to be grand. A good day, a kind word, a piece of work done well. The spinning slows when there's something in the middle. So today's practice is small. Not to stop all motion, just to stop one spinning thing. One tab, one loop of checking, one busy task that doesn't actually point anywhere. And in the time you get back, learn one good thing.
screen: `DO OUTSIDE THINGS DISTRACT YOU?` · `LEARN SOMETHING NEW AND GOOD.` · `BUSY, BUT AIMLESS, IS SPINNING TOO.` · `GIVE EVERY MOVE AN AIM.` · then, large: `STOP SPINNING.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Let the day's spinning come to mind: the checking, the switching, the half-done things. Don't fight them. Just watch them circle, like leaves in wind. Now find the center: one aim for today, simple and real. Let your breath settle around it. Then pick one spinning thing you'll stop when the bell rings, and one good thing you'll learn instead. The bell holds the time.
Stop being whirled around. Marcus's cure for distraction: learn something new and good, and give every movement an aim, so busyness isn't just more spinning. Today's word.
Your line: stop spinning. Close one tab, one loop, one aimless task today, and use the time to learn one good thing. Day five hundred thirty-three.

screen: `DAY 533 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: ATTEND TO YOUR OWN SOUL.`

howItsDone: Readers who take this entry to heart often set a single aim for the day and cut one habitual distraction, using the time to study something worthwhile.

fork.reveal: Marcus warns against both errors: being whirled around by outside things, and wearing yourself out with aimless activity.

trapdoor: what you thought: stop getting distracted.
what it means: two kinds of spinning, pushed by outside things or by aimless busyness; the cure is learning something good and having one aim.
what a scholar hears: the 'aim' (skopos) to which every impulse is directed is a recurring Stoic idea; Marcus returns to it throughout the notebook.

sources.quoted: Give thyself time to learn something new and good, and cease to be whirled around.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): the top and the leaf were attributed to Marcus, but 2.7 only says "whirled around"; the images are now the narrator's. Hook no longer tells the listener how they feel. Cut "Marcus was in an army camp" and the unsourced claim about what his aim was; replaced the myth about writing "in retirement" with one taken from the text.
Long 1862, 2.7 sentence quoted: confirm word for word.
Rest of 2.7 paraphrased: avoid being carried about the other way; triflers who weary themselves by activity yet have no object to direct every movement and thought. Confirm.
'skopos' as the Stoic term for the aim: confirm the Greek term used in 2.7.
